newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries continue downward spiral on Monday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries continue downward spiral on Monday.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities retreated further on Monday following Friday's sharp drop, as analysts said the market had been overpriced and a correction had been expected.

Bond prices had surged last week as market participants greeted weak inflationary news -- until Friday -- when nonfarm payrolls numbers for July came in far stronger than expected, leading to a dramatic fall in a market that had been growing at an intense pace. The market sagged further when the National Association of Purchasing Management reported numbers that suggested the U.S. manufacturing sector was strong.
"Everyone's trying to recalibrate and some may prefer to move in on the curve, said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist and vice president at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
The bond market may be held back in the face of supply in the near-term, said Peter Kretzmer, senior economist at Nationsbanc Capital Markets Inc.
However, he saw nothing fundamentally undermining the economy. Therefore, this week's auction should go well, he said.
"We do see the economy picking up in the third quarter, so yields could flatten some more," he said.
Kretzmer said Nationsbanc maintained a bullish outlook on the the economy in the long run. However, labor supply issues could pose a short-term threat, he said.
If, and when, the Federal reserve can ease monetary policy, yields on the long-term bond could remain at the 6.50 percent level, he said.

Stephen Slifer, chief economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc, said the market's reaction to Friday's news was out of proportion, noting that the aggregate hours worked index fell 0.5 in July and was back at second quarter levels, even with rises in overal employment of 200,000 or more.
He saw GDP growth of 2.5 to 3.0 percent in the third quarter -- a sustainable level in the eyes of Federal Reserve policymakers.

"GDP is not so troubling either," Slifer said. He said the large increase seen in inventories would not continue to grow and final sales growth of 2.5 percent in 1997 were nothing to get excited about.
The Fed refrained from adding reserves to the banking system on Monday during its usual midmorning intervention period.
The Treasury's 30-year bond was closing 13/32 lower at 101-28/32 to yield 6.48 percent.
The 10-year issue was at 102-29/32, off 9/32 to yield 6.22 percent. The five-year issue was down 5/32 at 99-17/32 to yield 6.11 percent. The two-year was 2/32 lower at 99-30/32 to yield 5.91 percent.
At the short end of the maturity spectrum, the three-month and year bills were unchanged at 5.14 and 5.22 percent, respectively. The six-month bill was one basis point higher at 5.19 percent.
